title: Features that change fastest between species are the most complex

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Features that change fastest between species are the most complex

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Among related species, the features that differ most rapidly (such as pigmentation and texture patterns) are the ones that show the most obvious complexity, while features under natural selection stay nearly constant.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it is almost always those features which change most rapidly between species that show the most obvious signs of complexity.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “Fundamental Issues in Biology” (from p. 383), p. 396. Scope: variation of traits among closely related species

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-16: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.53

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public images, morphology matrices, and phylogenies support analyses in selected clades. Coverage and trait homology are uneven, and the proposed contrast between rapid change and selection is causally problematic. Existing resources can test correlations but not the almost-always or causal components.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across related species, estimate phylogenetic rates for homologous traits, assign quantitative pattern-complexity scores, and test their association while separately estimating evidence of stabilizing or directional selection. The claim predicts a near-universal positive rate-complexity relationship and low rates for selected features.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Obvious complexity is observer- and metric-dependent.

Species differences do not directly measure evolutionary rate without dense phylogenies.

Rapid change can itself be driven by selection.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Phylogenies and image collections make a rate-versus-complexity comparison feasible for particular groups such as molluscs, fishes, or butterflies. Coverage is a subset of related species, and treating conservation as evidence of selection builds the conclusion into the measurement. The pattern can be tested where traits have been coded and not as a general biological rule.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Among species in a clade, estimate evolutionary rate for each trait and score trait complexity independently, then test whether the fastest traits are the most complex and the most conserved traits are those with independent evidence of selection. A positive rate-complexity relationship would support the claim; fast change in simple traits, or slow change in the most complex ones, would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Complexity scored from photographs is observer-dependent, and quantitative matrices exist for few clades.

Inferring selection from constancy makes the second clause circular.
